pnp

One-time pad file encryption that stays secure even if P = NP.

pnp encrypts any file with a key of truly random bytes as long as the file, read from your machine's hardware random number generators. A one-time pad doesn't rely on any problem being hard to compute, so no amount of computing power can break it.

pnp                      # browse your files and encrypt or decrypt them step by step
pnp photo.jpg            # writes photo.jpg.pnp and its key photo.jpg.pnp.key
pnp -d photo.jpg.pnp     # gives back photo.jpg

Without the key, nobody can read the file; with it, anyone can. So the weakest link is how you store your keys: keep them offline and apart from the .pnp files.

Install

For Debian 12 and newer, Ubuntu 22.04 and newer, and systems based on them (Linux Mint 21+, Kubuntu, KDE neon), on 64-bit PCs (amd64). One package works on all of them.

sudo install -d -m 0755 /etc/apt/keyrings
sudo wget -qO /etc/apt/keyrings/pnp.asc https://pnp.regulusarms.com/pnp.asc
printf 'Types: deb\nURIs: https://pnp.regulusarms.com/\nSuites: stable\nComponents: main\nSigned-By: /etc/apt/keyrings/pnp.asc\n' \
  | sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/pnp.sources
sudo apt update
sudo apt install pnp

Check the key you downloaded before trusting it: gpg --show-keys /etc/apt/keyrings/pnp.asc should show the fingerprint

B605 C24B 0B68 BEF1 3104  D104 8A29 1737 19C4 4365

For development builds, use Suites: dev instead of stable.

Let pnp read your hardware random generator

Only root can read /dev/hwrng by default. The package adds a pnp group that can; join it once, then log out and back in:

sudo usermod -aG pnp $USER

pnp --sources lists the hardware sources it found. pnp also uses the RDSEED instruction of Intel and AMD CPUs, which needs no setup. If no hardware source works, pnp refuses to encrypt.

If P = NP, build from source

pnp's encryption doesn't depend on P ≠ NP. The way you get pnp does. This repository is signed with an RSA key, and HTTPS and git rely on problems being hard to compute. If P = NP is proven with a practical algorithm, all of these could be forged, and apt would install a fake package.

No signature scheme is known to survive that. Until a P = NP-resistant way to sign and deliver software exists, the safest way to get pnp is to get its source from more than one place, read it (it's small, plain C with no libraries), and build it yourself: make, then sudo make install. Files you encrypted with an honest copy of pnp stay safe either way.
